q: What is molten rock called once it reaches the surface and flows out of a volcano?
note: The very same material is called magma while it is still underground.

q: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
note: It covers roughly a third of the planet's surface, which is more than all the land put together.

q: What is the name for a scientist who studies the weather?
note: The name has nothing to do with meteors, and comes from a Greek word for anything high in the sky.

q: What is the name for molten rock once it has reached the Earth’s surface?
note: The same material is called magma while it is still underground.

q: What is the main cause of the ocean's tides?
a: The gravitational pull of the Moon
note: The Sun tugs as well, and when the two line up you get the extra-large spring tides.

q: What is the name for a violently rotating column of air that reaches the ground?
note: When the same thing forms over water it is called a waterspout instead.

q: Which gas makes up roughly 78 percent of the Earth's atmosphere?
note: Oxygen accounts for about 21 percent, and everything else shares the small remainder.

q: What instrument is used to detect and record the shaking of an earthquake?
note: An early Chinese version, built in the second century, signalled a distant quake by dropping a ball from a dragon's mouth.

q: What type of rock is formed when molten rock cools and hardens?
note: The name comes from ignis, the Latin word for fire, and granite is a familiar example.

q: What is the Earth's thin, solid outermost layer called?
note: Beneath the oceans it can be as little as five kilometers thick, far thinner than under the continents.

q: What is the process called when water vapor cools and turns back into a liquid?
note: It is what forms clouds in the sky and beads of water on the outside of a cold glass.

q: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?
note: A sharp fall in pressure usually means unsettled weather is on the way.

q: What is the theory that the Earth's outer shell is broken into large, slowly moving slabs called?
note: The plates creep along at roughly the speed your fingernails grow.

q: What name is given to the supercontinent that geologists believe existed around 250 million years ago?
note: It began breaking apart in the Jurassic, eventually producing the continents we have now.

q: Marble forms when limestone is heated and squeezed underground, making it which of the three main rock types?
note: The word means changed in form, and slate is made from shale in much the same way.

q: What is the name for a huge ocean wave set off by an undersea earthquake or landslide?
note: Out in deep water it can pass under a ship almost unnoticed, only rearing up as it reaches shallow coast.

q: What is the name of the towering, anvil-topped cloud that brings thunderstorms?
note: It can climb more than ten kilometers, flattening out at the top when it hits the ceiling of the lower atmosphere.

q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ozone layer?
note: It sits above almost all the weather, which is why airliners like to cruise at its lower edge.

q: What name is given to the ancient supercontinent in which today's landmasses were all joined together?
note: It began breaking apart roughly 175 million years ago, and the pieces are still drifting today.

q: What is the name of the scale used to rank the hardness of minerals, running from talc up to diamond?
note: It is a ranking rather than a measurement, so the gap between nine and ten is enormous.
